title: Trump to Award Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II Moon Crew
excerpt: The four astronauts who completed the first crewed lunar mission in over 50 years will receive the highest US spaceflight distinction at a ceremony on August 28.
body:
• President Trump will present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to all four Artemis II crew members at NASA's Johnson Space Center on August 28.
  • The crew — Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen — completed a 10-day mission around the Moon in April, traveling farther than any humans in history.
  • Victor Glover became the first Black astronaut on a lunar mission, Christina Koch the first woman, and Jeremy Hansen the first Canadian to leave low-Earth orbit.
  • NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman also revealed Artemis III could launch as early as June 2027.

Highest Spaceflight Honor

President Donald Trump will award each member of NASA's Artemis II crew the Congressional Space Medal of Honor at a ceremony on August 28 at Johnson Space Center in Houston, NASA announced on August 21.

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor is the United States' highest distinction reserved for spaceflight veterans. It recognizes astronauts who have "distinguished himself or herself by exceptionally meritorious efforts and contributions to the welfare of the nation and mankind." Despite its name, the award is presented by the President based on the NASA Administrator's recommendation.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, will become the 31st through 34th recipients of the medal since Congress first authorized it in 1969.

A Mission of Historic Firsts

The Artemis II crew completed a 10-day mission around the Moon, splashing down on April 10. It was the first crewed flight of NASA's Orion spacecraft and the first time humans traveled beyond the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. The crew also set a new record for the farthest distance from Earth reached by humans.

The mission carried particular symbolic weight. Victor Glover became the first Black astronaut to participate in a lunar mission. Christina Koch became the first woman assigned to fly around the Moon. And Jeremy Hansen became the first Canadian — and first non-American — to leave low-Earth orbit.

"I think we can all agree there were no greater ambassadors to the stars than Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy. From selection through splashdown, they represented NASA and their nations with extraordinary professionalism and heart."

— Jared Isaacman, NASA Administrator

A Medal With Deep History

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was first awarded in 1978 to six Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo veterans including Alan Shepard, John Glenn, and Neil Armstrong. Other recipients include the crews of Apollo 13, the first space shuttle mission, and the fallen crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia.

The most recent previous recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, honored in 2023 for being the first NASA astronauts to launch on a commercial spacecraft.

Artemis III on the Horizon

The award ceremony comes as NASA accelerates its plans for Artemis III, the mission intended to return humans to the lunar surface. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on August 21 that the Artemis III Space Launch System rocket will roll out to Kennedy Space Center Pad 39B for a wet dress test before the end of 2026, with a launch planned for as early as June 2027.

The Artemis II astronauts have also been nominated for the Congressional Gold Medal, the highest civilian honor alongside the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Bipartisan legislation introduced in June by Senator Mark Kelly and Representative Don Bacon is awaiting votes in both the Senate and House.
